subskill: boundaries: semicolon after a clause whose subject is a that-clause
passage: That the comet sighted over the port city in 1661 and the one recorded by court astronomers more than a century earlier were the same object was not seriously proposed until the twentieth ______ calculations run on early electronic computers finally showed that both sightings fit a single elongated orbit.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "Century; orbital" is correct. The sentence opens with a long subject, "That the comet sighted... and the one recorded... were the same object," and its verb is "was not seriously proposed," so everything up to "century" is a complete independent clause. "Orbital calculations... finally showed that both sightings fit a single elongated orbit" is a second independent clause, and a semicolon correctly joins two independent clauses. "Century, orbital" joins the two independent clauses with only a comma, which is a comma splice. "Century orbital" runs the two clauses together with no punctuation at all. "Century; when orbital" turns the second part into a dependent clause beginning with "when"; nothing after it supplies a main clause, so the words after the semicolon are a fragment.

subskill: boundaries: semicolon before a clause opening with a participial phrase
passage: The hurricane that crossed the island in September 1928 toppled nearly every palm along its northern ______ of its bark and most of its crown, the great fig at the center of the botanical garden survived the storm and is still standing today.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "Shore; stripped" is correct. "The hurricane... toppled nearly every palm along its northern shore" is an independent clause. What follows is a second independent clause whose subject is "the great fig" and whose verbs are "survived" and "is"; it simply opens with the descriptive phrase "stripped of its bark and most of its crown." A semicolon correctly joins the two independent clauses. "Shore, stripped" joins them with only a comma, which is a comma splice, even though the phrase right after the comma looks as if it could describe the shore. "Shore stripped" runs the two clauses together with no punctuation. "Shore, though stripped" adds "though" to the opening phrase, but the second part is still a complete independent clause ("the great fig... survived"), so the two clauses are still joined by only a comma.

subskill: boundaries: no comma between a long subject and its verb
passage: The decision by the city's transit authority to replace its entire fleet of diesel buses with battery-electric models built by a single regional ______ more than a decade to carry out, largely because the power grid serving the bus depots had to be rebuilt before the first vehicles could be charged there overnight.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "Manufacturer eventually took" is correct. The subject of the sentence is "the decision," and everything from "by the city's transit authority" through "manufacturer" modifies it; the sentence needs a main verb for that subject, and "took" supplies it with no punctuation between subject and verb. "Manufacturer, which took" turns the verb into part of a relative clause describing the manufacturer, leaving "the decision" without a main verb, so the sentence is a fragment. "Manufacturer; this took" places a semicolon after a long noun phrase that is not an independent clause. "Manufacturer, and it took" joins the unfinished subject phrase to a new clause with "and," so "the decision" still never receives a verb.

subskill: boundaries: no comma after a parenthesis between subject and verb
passage: The original spillway of the reservoir above the old river town (a stepped concrete chute that the dam's engineers had redesigned twice before it was finally completed in ______ later replaced by a wider channel after new rainfall records showed that a once-in-a-century flood would overtop it by nearly two meters.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "1954) was" is correct. The subject of the sentence is "the original spillway of the reservoir above the old river town," and the parenthetical "(a stepped concrete chute that the dam's engineers had redesigned twice before it was finally completed in 1954)" adds detail about it. Once the parenthesis is closed, the main verb "was" follows directly, with no punctuation between the subject and its verb. "1954), was" adds a comma after the parenthesis, placing a comma between the subject and its verb. "1954) and was" makes "was later replaced" part of a compound with nothing before it to pair with, so "the original spillway" never receives a main verb and the sentence is a fragment. "1954, was" never closes the parenthesis that opens before "a stepped concrete chute."

subskill: boundaries: trailing although-clause attached to the clause before it
passage: The library scanned its collection of seventeenth-century harbor charts at the modest resolution its online catalog ______ conservators who had restored the charts argued that only a far sharper scan would capture the faint pencil soundings that later pilots had added in the margins.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "Required, although the" is correct. "The library scanned its collection... at the modest resolution its online catalog required" is an independent clause. "Although the conservators... argued that only a far sharper scan would capture the faint pencil soundings..." is a dependent clause: it begins with "although," and no main clause follows it. A comma correctly attaches this dependent clause to the end of the independent clause. "Required. Although the" makes the dependent clause its own sentence, which is a fragment. "Required; although the" uses a semicolon, which must join two independent clauses, but what follows it is a dependent clause with no main clause. "Required, and although the" uses "and" as if a second independent clause were coming, but after the "although" clause the sentence ends without one.

subskill: boundaries: commas between noun-phrase items in a series
passage: For each of the 212 wells in the district, the hydrologists recorded the depth to which the original casing had been ______ salinity of the water drawn during the dry season, and the date on which the well had last been cleaned.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "Sunk, the" is correct. The verb "recorded" has three objects in a series: "the depth to which the original casing had been sunk," "the salinity of the water drawn during the dry season," and "the date on which the well had last been cleaned." Items in a series that contain no internal commas are separated by commas, matching the comma after "season." "Sunk; the" puts a semicolon between the first two items but a comma between the second and third; semicolons separate series items only when the items themselves contain commas, and then they must be used between every item. "Sunk the" omits the comma between the first and second items, running them together. "Sunk: the" uses a colon, which would make "the salinity..." and "the date..." an explanation of "the depth" rather than further items in the list.

subskill: boundaries: two independent clauses, the second opening with "by then"
passage: The engineers spent nearly six years tunneling beneath the harbor with hand tools and compressed-air caissons, losing dozens of workers to decompression sickness along the ______ had already approved funding for a suspension bridge that would carry far more traffic and make the finished tunnel nearly obsolete.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: way, which by then the council
explanation: "Way. By then, the council" is correct. "The engineers spent nearly six years tunneling..." and "the council had already approved funding..." are both independent clauses, and a period correctly separates them; "by then" begins the second sentence and is followed by a comma. "Way, by then, the council" joins the two independent clauses with only a comma, which is a comma splice. "Way, which by then the council" introduces "which" but gives it no role in the clause that follows, since "approved" already has its object, "funding"; the result is ungrammatical. "Way by then, the council" attaches "by then" to the end of the first clause and then joins the second independent clause to it with only a comma, which is also a comma splice.

subskill: boundaries: comma before a sentence-final noun phrase summing up a clause
passage: After 140 years of continuous operation, the city's covered fish market was closed by a narrow vote of the council in the spring of ______ that the vendors, many of whose families had held the same stalls since the 1880s, protested for months on the steps of city hall.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "2009, a decision" is correct. "The city's covered fish market was closed by a narrow vote of the council in the spring of 2009" is an independent clause. "A decision that the vendors... protested for months" is a noun phrase that renames the event the clause describes; "protested" belongs to the clause beginning with "that," so the phrase has no main verb of its own. A comma correctly attaches such a phrase to the end of the clause. "2009. A decision" makes the noun phrase its own sentence, which is a fragment. "2009; a decision" uses a semicolon, which must join two independent clauses, before a phrase that is not a clause. "2009, it was a decision" turns the phrase into a second independent clause with "it was" and joins it to the first with only a comma, a comma splice.

subskill: boundaries: no mark between a verb and its delayed object
passage: The conservators, working with cotton swabs and a solvent gel mild enough to leave the original paint untouched, slowly removed from the altarpiece's gilded ______ layers of darkened varnish, each one applied by a different restorer during the previous three centuries.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "Frame three" is correct. The verb "removed" needs an object, and here the object, "three layers of darkened varnish," comes after the phrase "from the altarpiece's gilded frame." No punctuation belongs between a verb and its object, even when a phrase separates them. "Frame, three" puts a comma between "removed from the altarpiece's gilded frame" and the object of "removed." "Frame. Three" ends the first sentence before "removed" has an object and leaves "Three layers of darkened varnish, each one applied..." as a fragment with no verb. "Frame: three" uses a colon, but a colon must follow a complete independent clause, and "the conservators... slowly removed from the altarpiece's gilded frame" is not complete without its object.

subskill: boundaries: name after a descriptor that already identifies one person
passage: In 1902 the museum entrusted its newly purchased tablets to the only member of its staff who could read cuneiform ______ Hartmann, and it was his transliterations, published four years later, that first revealed the archive to be a merchant family's correspondence.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "Script, Ernst" is correct. "The only member of its staff who could read cuneiform script" already identifies exactly one person, so the name "Ernst Hartmann" adds information rather than identifying him, and it is set off by a pair of commas; the second comma, after "Hartmann," also comes before "and it was." "Script Ernst" treats the name as needed to tell which staff member is meant, but the phrase "the only member" has already done that. "Script; Ernst" uses a semicolon, which must join two independent clauses, but "Ernst Hartmann" is only a name, not a clause. "Script, and Ernst" makes "Ernst Hartmann" a second person the tablets were entrusted to, and the sentence then runs on into ", and it was his transliterations..." with nothing to connect it.

subskill: boundaries: comma and conjunction before a clause opening with "when"
passage: The river overtopped its levees three times during the unusually wet spring of ______ water finally receded in early June, farmers in the lower valley found their fields buried under nearly a meter of silt.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "1927, and when the" is correct. "The river overtopped its levees three times during the unusually wet spring of 1927" is an independent clause, and "farmers in the lower valley found their fields buried..." is a second independent clause that opens with the dependent clause "when the water finally receded in early June." A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction "and" correctly joins the two independent clauses. "1927, when the" and "1927 when the" both attach the "when" clause to the first clause and then join "farmers... found" to it with only a comma, a comma splice. "1927, then when the" also uses only a comma to join the two independent clauses; "then" is an adverb, not a conjunction, so it cannot join them.

subskill: boundaries: colon after an independent clause before a noun phrase
passage: After cataloguing more than six hundred clay tablets recovered from the palace archive, the epigraphers concluded that the scribes had relied on a single standard for every length they ______ royal cubit, a bronze rod kept in the temple of the city god and copied onto wooden measuring sticks for officials in each province.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "Recorded: the" is correct. "The epigraphers concluded that the scribes had relied on a single standard for every length they recorded" is a complete independent clause, and what follows names that standard; a colon correctly introduces an explanation or specification after an independent clause, even when what follows is only a noun phrase. "Recorded the" leaves no break, so "the royal cubit" reads as the object of "recorded," which already has its object in "every length"; the sentence becomes ungrammatical. "Recorded, and the" uses "and" to begin a second clause, but "the royal cubit, a bronze rod kept... and copied..." has no verb, so nothing completes it. "Recorded. The" makes "The royal cubit, a bronze rod kept... and copied..." a separate sentence, but it has no main verb, so it is a fragment.

subskill: boundaries: long introductory prepositional phrase kept whole
passage: Throughout the four years of negotiations between the upstream and downstream ______ insisted on publishing every draft of the proposed compact, a practice that slowed the talks considerably but made it nearly impossible for either side to claim afterward that it had been misled about the terms.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: states over water rights, federal mediators
states, over water rights, federal mediators
states over water rights; federal mediators
correct_answer: states over water rights, federal mediators
explanation: "States over water rights, federal mediators" is correct. The sentence opens with one long prepositional phrase, "Throughout the four years of negotiations between the upstream and downstream states over water rights"; "over water rights" tells which negotiations are meant, so it belongs inside that phrase. A single comma marks the end of the whole introductory phrase, just before the subject "federal mediators." "States, over water rights, federal mediators" sets "over water rights" off with a pair of commas as if it were removable extra information, but it is an essential part of the phrase that identifies the negotiations. "States over water rights—federal mediators" uses a single dash, which is not used to end an introductory phrase. "States over water rights; federal mediators" uses a semicolon, which must join two independent clauses, after a phrase that is not a clause.

subskill: form: finite verb for a subject followed by a reduced relative clause
passage: Ecologists studying old-growth forests have found that fungal threads link the roots of neighboring trees and that the network they form ______ sugars from tall, sunlit trees to seedlings growing in deep shade, a transfer that may help young firs survive their first decade.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The blank falls inside a clause introduced by "that": "that the network they form ______ sugars." The subject of this clause is "the network," and "they form" is a shortened relative clause describing it ("the network [that] they form"). "Network" still needs a verb of its own, and because it is singular, that verb must be singular: "redistributes." "Redistribute" is plural; it agrees with "they" or "threads," which come just before the blank, rather than with "network." "And redistribute" joins a second verb to "form," so both verbs belong to "they," and "the network" is left with no verb at all. "Redistributing" is a participle, not a finite verb, so it also leaves "the network" without a verb.

subskill: form: plural possessive with number set by an earlier sentence
passage: Starting in 2011, two ornithologists kept one shared handwritten log of the arrival date of every barn swallow that nested under the eaves of a dairy barn in rural Ontario. Over thirteen years, the ______ grew to more than 9,000 entries, and it now shows that the birds arrive nearly a week earlier than they once did.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The first sentence establishes two facts: two ornithologists kept the record, and they kept one shared log. The possessive must therefore be plural, "ornithologists'" (plural noun, apostrophe after the s), and the noun must be singular, "log." "Ornithologists' log" gets both right, and it also matches the singular pronoun "it" later in the sentence. "Ornithologist's log" uses a singular possessive, which credits the record to only one person. "Ornithologist's logs" makes that same error and also makes the noun plural. "Ornithologists' logs" uses the correct possessive, but the plural "logs" contradicts the one shared log described in the first sentence and clashes with "it."

subskill: form: agreement with a gerund-phrase subject containing plural nouns
passage: Reintroducing gray wolves to the northern ranges of the park after an absence of nearly seventy years ______ the grazing patterns of elk herds, which now avoid the open riverbanks where young willows have begun to recover.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The subject of this sentence is the gerund phrase "Reintroducing gray wolves to the northern ranges of the park after an absence of nearly seventy years." A gerund phrase names a single action, so it takes a singular verb even though it contains the plural nouns "wolves," "ranges," and "years." "Has reshaped" is a singular finite verb, and its present perfect tense links the past reintroduction to the present, where the elk "now avoid" the riverbanks. "Have reshaped" is plural; it agrees with one of the plural nouns inside the phrase rather than with the phrase itself. "Reshaping" is a participle, so it leaves the subject without a main verb and turns the sentence into a fragment. "Had reshaped" uses the past perfect, which places an action before some other moment in the past; no such moment appears here, and the sentence goes on to describe what the elk do "now."

subskill: modifier: opening modifier must attach to the noun after the comma
passage: Last spring a ceremonial robe was returned to the coastal community where it had been made, after more than a century in private collections. Woven from the inner bark of yellow cedar and the wool of mountain goats and patterned with rows of stylized ravens, ______
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: the community now displays the robe in its longhouse.
the robe now hangs in the community's longhouse.
the robe's ravens now look out over the longhouse.
the longhouse now holds the robe at its center.
correct_answer: the robe now hangs in the community's longhouse.
explanation: The second sentence opens with a long modifier: "Woven from the inner bark of yellow cedar and the wool of mountain goats and patterned with rows of stylized ravens." A modifier in this position describes the noun that comes right after the comma, so that noun must be the thing that was woven and patterned: the robe. "The robe now hangs in the community's longhouse" puts "the robe" right after the modifier. "The community now displays the robe in its longhouse" makes the community the thing woven from cedar bark and goat wool. "The robe's ravens now look out over the longhouse" makes "ravens" the subject; "robe's" is only a possessive, and the ravens are not what was patterned with rows of ravens. "The longhouse now holds the robe at its center" says that the longhouse was woven and patterned.
